query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, controlled addition of boron (0.5–1.5 at%) to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will lead to the in situ formation of finely dispersed boride precipitates (e.g., TiB2 or NiB) that bolster grain boundary cohesion and hinder dislocation motion during high-temperature deformation, thus improving elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the same alloy without boron.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements with titanium and nickel as the primary constituents (e.g., approximately 40–50 at% Ti, 30–40 at% Ni, and the balance made up of three or more additional elements each in the range of 5–35 at%).
generation.intervention: Microalloying with a trace addition (0.5–1.5 at%) of boron during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing conditions (e.g., tests conducted at 600–800°C under tensile or creep loads) where the alloy is expected to serve in extreme environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, dispersed boride precipitates (such as TiB2 or NiB) at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Boron encourages the nucleation of stable boride phases which, by precipitating at grain boundaries, act to pin these boundaries and impede dislocation motion. This dispersion strengthening mechanism is expected to enhance yield strength and delay creep under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped alloy will show increased yield strength and lower creep rates at elevated temperatures compared to an otherwise identical alloy without boron, as a result of the enhanced grain boundary stability.
generation.baseline: The same high-entropy alloy composition without any boron addition.
generation.boundary: The effects are expected within the compositional confines of high-entropy alloys (each element present at 5–35 at%) and during high-temperature operation (around 600–800°C), below temperatures at which new phase transformations could occur.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal boron concentration and the full range of its effects remain uncertain, as elemental interactions and processing conditions could influence both the size and distribution of boride precipitates. Further experimental determination is necessary to optimize these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy, and another set with the addition of 0.5–1.5 at% boron. Perform identical processing to ensure comparable microstructures aside from boron content. Subject both sets to high-temperature mechanical tests (such as creep and tensile tests at 600–800°C) and carry out detailed microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM/SEM) to verify the presence and distribution of boride precipitates.
measurements: Grain boundary precipitate size, density, and distribution via microscopic analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (for example, less than a 15% increase in high-temperature yield strength and/or no reduction in creep rate) relative to the baseline samples, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the expected fine boride precipitates, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
